content: Previous Cochrane Reviews have demonstrated that cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for anxiety disorders in children and adolescents. However, there are still unresolved questions regarding its relative efficacy and acceptability compared to other interventions, such as waiting lists or no treatment, treatment as usual (TAU), attention controls, and alternative treatments. Additionally, there is limited understanding of its benefits across various outcomes, its long-term effects, its effectiveness in different delivery formats, and its impact on children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) or intellectual impairments. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of CBT for childhood anxiety disorders in comparison to waitlist/no treatment, TAU, attention control, alternative treatments, and medication. The primary outcomes assessed were the remission of the primary anxiety diagnosis after treatment and the acceptability of the intervention, measured by the number of participants lost to follow-up. Secondary outcomes included remission of all anxiety diagnoses, reduction in anxiety and depressive symptoms, improvement in global functioning, adverse effects, and long-term effects. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Common Mental Disorders Controlled Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, up to October 2019. They also searched international trial registries and grey literature. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving direct contact with the child, parent, or both were included, provided they compared CBT to non-CBT interventions. Participants were under 19 years of age and met diagnostic criteria for an anxiety disorder. A total of 87 studies involving 5,964 participants were included in the quantitative analyses. Compared to waitlist/no treatment, CBT likely increases the remission of primary anxiety diagnoses post-treatment, with 49.4% of participants in the CBT group achieving remission compared to 17.8% in the waitlist/no treatment group. The odds ratio (OR) was 5.45 (95% confidence interval [CI] 3.90 to 7.60), with a number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) of 3. CBT also likely increases remission of all anxiety diagnoses (OR 4.43, 95% CI 2.89 to 6.78). The quality of evidence for these findings was moderate. When compared to TAU, low-quality evidence did not show a significant difference in remission of primary anxiety disorders post-treatment (OR 3.19, 95% CI 0.90 to 11.29). However, CBT may increase remission of all anxiety disorders compared to TAU (OR 2.74, 95% CI 1.16 to 6.46). Similarly, when compared to attention control, CBT may increase remission of primary anxiety disorders (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.33 to 3.89) and all anxiety disorders (OR 2.75, 95% CI 1.22 to 6.17), although the quality of evidence was low. There was insufficient data to compare CBT to alternative treatments for remission of primary anxiety disorders. Low-quality evidence suggested little to no difference between CBT and alternative treatments in remission of all anxiety disorders (OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.23). Regarding acceptability, low-quality evidence showed no significant differences between CBT and waitlist/no treatment (OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.41), TAU (OR 1.37, 95% CI 0.73 to 2.56), attention control (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.49), or alternative treatments (OR 1.58, 95% CI 0.61 to 4.13). No adverse effects were reported across the included studies. However, in the few studies that mentioned adverse effects, it was unclear whether these were systematically monitored. The results for anxiety symptom outcomes, broader outcomes, long-term outcomes, and subgroup analyses are detailed in the full text. There was no consistent evidence of differences in outcomes based on delivery formats (e.g., individual versus group therapy or varying levels of therapist contact) or between children with and without ASD. No studies included children with intellectual impairments. In conclusion, CBT is likely more effective in the short term than waiting lists or no treatment and may be more effective than attention control. However, there is little to no evidence to suggest that CBT is superior to usual care or alternative treatments across outcomes. The confidence in these findings is limited due to concerns about the quality and quantity of available evidence. Further research is needed to determine the most efficient ways to improve outcomes for children and adolescents with anxiety disorders.
